questions.question: State the rules for assigning oxidation numbers. Find the oxidation number of Mn in KMnO₄ and Cr in K₂Cr₂O₇.
questions.solution:
Key rules: free elements 0; Group 1 +1, Group 2 +2; O usually −2 (peroxides −1); H usually +1 (hydrides −1); F always −1; the sum equals the species' charge.

KMnO₄: +1 + Mn + 4(−2) = 0 → Mn = **+7**.

K₂Cr₂O₇: 2(+1) + 2Cr + 7(−2) = 0 → Cr = **+6**.
questions.knowledgeNote: Maximum oxidation states (+7 Mn, +6 Cr, +6 S) mark the strongest oxidising agents of each family.

questions.question: Balance the redox reaction by the ion-electron method: MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ (acidic medium).
questions.solution:
Reduction: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O.

Oxidation: Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻ (×5).

Adding: **MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O**.

Check: charge −1+10+8 = +17 each side; atoms: Mn 1, Fe 5, H 8, O 4 ✓.
questions.knowledgeNote: Balance atoms (O via H₂O, H via H⁺) first, charges with electrons last — the order that prevents most errors.

questions.question: Define oxidising and reducing agents. Identify each in: Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu.
questions.solution:
**Oxidising agent** gains electrons (is itself reduced); **reducing agent** loses electrons (is itself oxidised).

Zn → Zn²⁺ + 2e⁻ (oxidised) so **Zn is the reductant**; Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu (reduced) so **CuSO₄ (Cu²⁺) is the oxidant**.
questions.knowledgeNote: 'OIL RIG' — Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons).

questions.question: What is the electrochemical series? Explain why zinc displaces copper from copper sulphate solution.
questions.solution:
The **electrochemical series** orders electrodes by standard reduction potential — higher (more positive) means easier to reduce.

Zn²⁺/Zn (−0.76 V) sits below Cu²⁺/Cu (+0.34 V): zinc is the stronger reductant, so Zn reduces Cu²⁺ to copper metal spontaneously.
questions.knowledgeNote: Any metal displaces metals below it in the series — the single rule behind all displacement predictions.

questions.question: Hydrogen peroxide can act both as an oxidising and a reducing agent. Explain with one reaction of each type.
questions.solution:
O in H₂O₂ is at −1, midway between O₂ (0) and H₂O (−2), so it can move either way.

**Oxidant:** H₂O₂ + 2KI + H₂SO₄ → I₂ + K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O (O: −1 → −2).

**Reductant:** 5H₂O₂ + 2KMnO₄ + 3H₂SO₄ → K₂SO₄ + 2MnSO₄ + 8H₂O + 5O₂ (O: −1 → 0).
questions.knowledgeNote: Intermediate oxidation states (−1 O, +4 S, +3 N) are the dual-role suspects — check them first.

questions.question: Why is fluorine the strongest oxidising agent among the halogens?
questions.solution:
Oxidising strength follows electron gain enthalpy and small size: F₂ has the highest electronegativity (4.0), the most exothermic electron affinity for its size, and a weak F–F bond that breaks easily.

So F₂ oxidises even water (to O₂) and displaces every other halogen — strength falls F₂ > Cl₂ > Br₂ > I₂.
questions.knowledgeNote: Standard potentials confirm it: F₂/F⁻ (+2.87 V) tops the whole electrochemical series.
